items.stem: Tomás uses u = eˣ + 6 to write ∫ eˣ/(eˣ + 6) dx as ∫ 1/u du without changing dx. Explain what is missing.
items.answer: dx must be replaced using du = eˣ dx; the correct integrand is 1/u.
items.markingKey: B1 must use du = eˣ dx; B1 correct integrand 1/u [2]

items.stem: Daniel uses u = x + 4 and writes ∫ x/√(x + 4) dx as ∫ x/√u du, leaving an x in the integrand. Explain how to complete the substitution.
items.answer: Every x must be written in terms of u: x = u − 4, and du = dx; the integrand becomes (u − 4)/√u.
items.markingKey: B1 x = u − 4; B1 correct integrand (u − 4)/√u [2]

items.stem: By differentiating (1/2)x² ln x − (1/4)x², show that it is an integral of x ln x.
items.answer: The product rule gives terms that cancel, leaving x ln x.
items.markingKey: M1 product rule; A1 simplifies to the integrand [2]

items.stem: Hana tries to find ∫ ln x/x² dx by parts with u = 1/x² and dv/dx = ln x, and finds that the new integral is harder than the original. Explain why, and state a better choice.
items.answer: Integrating ln x raises its power (or is hard), while differentiating 1/x² does not simplify it; take u = ln x and dv/dx = 1/x², giving −(ln x)/x − 1/x + c.
items.markingKey: B1 explains why the new integral is harder; B1 correct choice of u and dv/dx [2]

items.stem: Show that ∫ from 2 to 5 of (8x² + 44x + 56)/((x − 1)(x + 5)²) dx = −9/35 + 11 ln 2 + 5 ln 5 − 5 ln 7.

items.markingKey: M1 partial fractions; M1 integrates to logarithms; A1 uses limits to obtain the given answer [3]
